pickup.name: Busan subway pickup (3 stations)
pickup.category: Pickup — three central Busan SUBWAY stations (not the railway station)
pickup.description:
Pickup runs in sequence at **three subway stations** in central Busan: **Busan Station Exit 4 (Subway Line 1) — 08:10**, **Seomyeon Station Exit 4 (Subway Lines 1 & 2) — 08:30**, **Haeundae Station Exit 5 (Subway Line 2) — 09:10**. 

**All three points are subway station exits.** At Busan Station in particular we meet you at **Exit 4 of the Line 1 subway station in front of the building — NOT inside the KTX railway terminal**: if you wait in the train station concourse you will not see the vehicle. Please remember the subway exit numbers exactly as written (Busan Station Exit 4 · Seomyeon Station Exit 4 · Haeundae Station Exit 5). 

Pickup runs west→east, and after the final Haeundae stop we head north on the **Gyeongbu Expressway** toward Gyeongju, the ancient capital of **Silla (57 BCE – 935 CE)** — the longest-ruling dynasty in Korean history. The first destination, Ahopsan Bamboo Forest in Gijang-gun, is about 30 minutes from Haeundae.

pickup.whyOnRoute: The three pickup points cover Busan's main hotel clusters (Busan Station/Choryang, mid-city Seomyeon, and the Haeundae beachfront) evenly across Subway Lines 1 and 2, so guests never have to cross the city early in the morning. The reason all three are stated as **subway exits** is simple: the Busan Station plaza mixes trains, buses and taxis and makes a vehicle hard to identify, while a subway exit number is something anyone finds in one go. Running west→east minimizes coach distance and lands the group at Ahopsan around 09:40 — early enough that the bamboo forest is at its quietest and most photogenic.

gyochon.name: Gyochon Hanok Village & Choi Family House & Woljeonggyo Bridge
gyochon.category: Joseon head-family hanok village + reconstructed Silla wooden bridge (one drop-off, walked)
gyochon.description:
**Gyochon Hanok Village** and **Woljeonggyo Bridge** face each other across the Namcheon River, linked by a **10–15 minute riverside walk**, so this tour makes **one single drop-off and walks both**. 

The heart of **Gyochon** is the **Choi Family House — the head house of the Gyeongju Choi clan**, a merchant-aristocrat family that **held its wealth across 12 generations and 300 years** in the late Joseon era, and is designated **Important Folklore Material No. 27**. The family's six house rules (**never amass wealth beyond 10,000 sok**, **never buy up another's fields in a famine year**, **let no one within a hundred li starve**, and three more) are Korea's best-known example of noblesse oblige. The clan's liquor, **Gyodong Beopju, is Important Intangible Cultural Asset No. 86-3**, brewed inside the head house to a **350-year-old recipe** and sold on site (about ₩30,000 for a 750 ml bottle as of 2026). Right beside the village stand **Gyeongjuhyanggyo** (the Joseon-era regional Confucian academy) and the **site of Yoseokgung** — the residence of 7th-century Silla Princess Yoseok, daughter of King Muyeol and **mother of Seol Chong**, the monk-scholar who codified the Idu writing system. 

Across the river, **Woljeonggyo is Korea's largest fully wooden bridge**. The **Samguk Sagi** records its construction in **760 CE, under King Gyeongdeok, the 35th ruler of Silla**. Lost during the Joseon Dynasty, it was **excavated in 1984–1986, its main span reconstructed in 2008–2013, and two gatehouses added in 2016–2018**, reopening in **April 2018** — **1,258 years after it was first built**. The span measures **60.57 m long and 13 m wide**, and the reconstruction used **traditional Korean hanok timber joinery with no modern metal fasteners**. It was **designated a Historic Site in 2004** and named one of the **'100 Best Tourist Attractions in Korea 2025–2026'** by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism. 

**Both places are free to enter** (a few individual houses inside the village charge their own ₩2,000–3,000). The village fills with **cherry blossoms in early April** and **golden ginkgos in late October**.

gyochon.whyOnRoute: After lunch this is where the day shifts **from the grand royal-Buddhist scale of Bulguksa to the scale of lived history** — Gyeongju seen through a merchant family's eyes rather than a king's. The two places are bundled into one stop because the geography already does it: the southern edge of Gyochon **is** the north bank of Woljeonggyo, so **there is no reason to park twice**, and the time saved on boarding becomes time on foot. The 75-minute block lets you do both the Beopju tasting and the photos on the bridge without hurrying. Mid-afternoon is also when Woljeonggyo shows its **timber detail and river reflections most clearly in daylight**, and you avoid the crowd that gathers at sunset.

daereungwon.name: Daereungwon Tomb Complex & Hwangnidan-gil
daereungwon.category: Silla royal tomb park + hanok cafe street (walked, one drop-off)
daereungwon.description:
**Daereungwon** is a tomb park of **126,500 m²** of gentle grass mounds holding **23 tombs of Silla kings, queens and nobles**, most of them raised in the **4th–6th centuries**. The most famous is **Cheonmachong (Tomb 155)** — **excavated on April 16, 1973**, 12.7 m high and about 47 m across, and **the only tomb in Daereungwon whose interior is open to visitors**. The dig produced **11,526 artifacts**, among them the **Cheonmachong Gold Crown (National Treasure No. 188)** and the **Cheonmado — the only Silla-era painting that survives**, drawn on a birch-bark saddle flap (the crown itself is on display later in the day, at Gyeongju National Museum). Neighbouring **Hwangnamdaechong** is the largest tomb in the complex: its twin north and south mounds hold **an unidentified Silla king and queen buried together**, and the queen's gold crown carries **3 pairs** of pendants where a king's normally carries one — a hint at how high Silla's early royal women stood. **Park admission is free** (Cheonmachong's interior costs adult ₩3,000 / youth ₩2,000 / child ₩1,000). Climbing the mounds is prohibited. 

**Directly across Daereungwon's west wall** is **Hwangnidan-gil**. The name fuses **Hwangnam-dong with Gyeongnidan-gil** (Seoul's Itaewon street) — it literally means **'Hwangnam-dong's Gyeongnidan-gil'**. Running **from Naenam Intersection to the Hwangnam Elementary School intersection**, both sides are lined with **cafes, restaurants, studios and gift shops converted out of hanok houses**, and **since around 2017** it has been the youngest street in Gyeongju. This neighbourhood is also the home of **Hwangnam bread** — the thin wheat pastry filled with red-bean paste **first made in 1939 in Hwangnam-dong by Choi Yeong-hwa**, and the souvenir travellers carry out of Gyeongju more than any other. 

Because tombs and cafe street are separated by **a single wall**, this tour walks **1,500 years and the 2020s side by side on one drop-off**.

daereungwon.whyOnRoute: After the Joseon-and-Silla heritage block of Gyochon and Woljeonggyo, this is **the one stop of the day in the present tense**. Daereungwon has no stairs and no climb — flat grass paths make it the easiest walking of the day — and one wall further on there is coffee and red-bean bread on Hwangnidan-gil. The fact that **a royal tomb and a cafe are a one-minute walk apart** is itself the character of this city. Late afternoon is when Hwangnidan-gil is at its liveliest, and it lets guests handle **restrooms, coffee and souvenirs in one place** before the final stop (the museum, or Donggung & Wolji). The **actual** gold crown is at Gyeongju National Museum, the next stop — so seeing the excavation site at Cheonmachong and then the artifact at the museum makes **the order itself the story**.

museum.name: Gyeongju National Museum (in winter, Donggung & Wolji by night)
museum.category: National museum of Silla artifacts — replaced Nov–Feb by the Donggung & Wolji night view
museum.description:
The last stop of the day is one of two, depending on the season. 

**① Mar–Oct — Gyeongju National Museum (default).** **Korea's premier museum of Silla artifacts**, founded as a branch museum in **1945**, with the main building opened in **1968** and **National Museum status granted in 1975**. The collection runs to **over 100,000 items, including more than 30,000 designated Cultural Heritage pieces**. The core exhibits are **(1) the Cheonmachong Gold Crown (National Treasure No. 188)** — the very object taken from the tomb you saw at Daereungwon, unearthed in 1973 — and **(2) the Sacred Bell of King Seongdeok, the Emille Bell (National Treasure No. 29)** — cast in **771 CE**, about 19 tons, one of the largest bronze bells still in existence (the legend that a child was cast into it was laid to rest as folklore when **alloy analysis in 1998 found no human remains**). The **Wolji Hall** displays **more than 33,000 artifacts recovered when Wolji (Anapji) was dredged in 1975–1976** — wooden objects, roof tiles and the famous drinking-game die, preserved in oxygen-starved mud — which pairs it directly with Donggung & Wolji next door. **Hours 10:00–18:00 (last admission 17:30); regular closures are Jan 1, Seollal and Chuseok only, and it is open as normal on Mondays. Permanent exhibitions are free.** From March to October it stays open until 20:00 on Saturdays. 

**② Nov–Feb — Donggung & Wolji (winter night view).** In winter the sun is already low by about 17:00, so at the same hour we go instead to **Gyeongju's finest night view**. **Donggung & Wolji (formerly Anapji, Historic Site No. 18)** is the **detached palace and pond of the Silla royal court, created in 674 by King Munmu**, famous for its pavilions mirrored on the water — and the 33,000-plus artifacts in the Wolji Hall above came from the bed of this very pond. **09:00–22:00 (ticketing closes 21:30), open every day of the year. Admission adult ₩3,000 / youth and soldiers ₩2,000 / child ₩1,000.** Winter sunset falls at around **17:15–17:30**, so this tour's arrival time (about 17:00) puts you there **from dusk through to the moment the lights come on**. 

The two sites are **5 minutes apart by car**, and your guide will confirm which one applies on the day, based on the season, the sunset time and conditions on the ground.

**Wolji Hall = 33,000+ artifacts from the 1975–1976 dredging of Wolji** — the twin of Donggung & Wolji

museum.whyOnRoute: Seeing the **actual gold crown** immediately after standing at the excavation site in Daereungwon closes the day as a single sentence: **tomb → artifact**. Putting it last comes out of the arithmetic — an arrival around 17:00 is **30 minutes ahead of the museum's 17:30 last admission**, with room to take in the highlights before the 18:00 close (this is a highlight loop around the gold crown, the Emille Bell and the Wolji Hall, not a sweep of the whole museum). And **in winter that same hour is the night-view hour instead**, so from November to February we head five minutes down the road to Donggung & Wolji — a picture the summer timetable simply cannot produce. Both options are flat walking, which makes them an easy last stop after a long day.

Around 70–80 minutes depending on traffic. Expected drop-off times are **Haeundae Station ≈19:15 · Seomyeon Station ≈19:35 · Busan Station ≈19:50**. 

The drop-off points are **the same subway exits you boarded at in the morning** — and Busan Station means the Line 1 subway station Exit 4, not the KTX railway terminal.

routeShapeSubtitle: A year-round day trip that starts in Busan and walks Gyeongju in a single day. The morning is two places reached by road (Ahopsan Bamboo Forest and Bulguksa); the afternoon is two blocks walked with the van parked — from Gyochon Hanok Village and the Choi Family House across the Namcheon to Woljeonggyo, and from the Daereungwon tombs over one wall into Hwangnidan-gil. The last slot belongs to the season: March to October it is Gyeongju National Museum, where the actual crown from the tomb you just walked through is on display, and November to February that same hour is the night-view hour, so it becomes Donggung & Wolji. Built for travellers who care less about how many sights they ticked off than about how long they got to stay at each one.

seo.description: A small-group mini-van day tour from Busan to Gyeongju. The day opens on the bamboo paths of Ahopsan Bamboo Forest, takes UNESCO World Heritage Bulguksa Temple at an unhurried pace, and then spends the afternoon on two blocks covered entirely on foot — Gyochon Hanok Village and the Choi Family House across to Woljeonggyo Bridge, and the Daereungwon royal tombs across to the Hwangnidan-gil cafe street. It finishes at Gyeongju National Museum (Cheonmachong Gold Crown, Emille Bell), which in winter (Nov–Feb) is replaced at the same hour by the Donggung & Wolji night view. Pickup and drop-off are Busan Station Exit 4, Seomyeon Station Exit 4 and Haeundae Station Exit 5 — all subway stations.

catalog.subtitle: Small-group mini-van · English-speaking guide — Ahopsan Bamboo Forest, Bulguksa (UNESCO), Gyochon Hanok Village + Choi Family House + Woljeonggyo, Daereungwon + Hwangnidan-gil, and Gyeongju National Museum (Donggung & Wolji night view in winter), all in one day.
catalog.shortCardDescription: A small-group Gyeongju day tour leaving from three Busan subway stations. The afternoon is walked with the van parked — Choi Family House to Woljeonggyo, Daereungwon to Hwangnidan-gil. It ends at Gyeongju National Museum, or at the Donggung & Wolji night view in winter.

whyItems.label: The afternoon is bundled into two blocks walked with the van parked
whyItems.detail: Gyochon Hanok Village and the Choi Family House are a 10–15 minute riverside walk from Woljeonggyo along the Namcheon, and Daereungwon and Hwangnidan-gil are separated by a single wall. So instead of four stops for four places we make only two drop-offs — the time that used to go into boarding and unboarding becomes walking time, and each block gets 75 minutes.

whyItems.label: The season decides the last slot — museum or night view
whyItems.detail: From March to October we reach Gyeongju National Museum at about 17:00 (30 minutes ahead of its 17:30 last admission). From November to February the sun is already going down at that same hour, so we drive five minutes to Donggung & Wolji instead and watch it from dusk through to the moment the lights come on. It is a picture the summer timetable cannot make.

whyItems.label: See it at the tomb, then see it again at the museum
whyItems.detail: You stand at the 1973 excavation site inside Cheonmachong at Daereungwon, and then meet the actual Cheonmachong Gold Crown (National Treasure No. 188) from that tomb at the next stop, Gyeongju National Museum. The same goes for the 33,000-plus artifacts in the Wolji Hall — they came out of the bed of the pond at Donggung & Wolji, the winter alternate. The order itself does the explaining.

whyItems.label: Every pickup point is a subway station exit
whyItems.detail: Busan Station Exit 4 (Line 1), Seomyeon Station Exit 4 (Lines 1 & 2), Haeundae Station Exit 5 (Line 2). At Busan Station in particular, we meet at Exit 4 of the subway station in front of the building, not inside the KTX railway terminal — the train station plaza mixes buses and taxis and makes a vehicle hard to find, while a subway exit number is something anyone finds in one go. Drop-off is at the same three points.

whyItems.label: Mini-van size, between a coach and a private car
whyItems.detail: Coach tours from Busan carry 35–45 passengers cheaply; private tours carry 1–4 at a much higher rate. This small-group mini-van sits between the two — fewer people means faster reassembly at each stop, and that time turns straight back into time on site.

seasonal.season: Spring (mid-Mar to mid-Apr, cherry blossom season)
seasonal.description: The Ahopsan opener swaps for the Haeundae Dalmaji Hill cherry-blossom road. Daereungwon's stone-wall lane is one of Gyeongju's finest cherry tunnels (with a festival in early April every year), and Gyochon village blossoms in early April too. The last stop is Gyeongju National Museum.

The bamboo forest stays cool and the museum is air-conditioned. Both afternoon walking blocks have shade and cafes to rest in. Sunset is around 19:30, so a night view does not fit the route and the last stop stays Gyeongju National Museum.

Gyochon's ginkgos peak in late October, and the grass mounds of Daereungwon make the easiest walking of the day. The last stop is Gyeongju National Museum, which from March to October stays open until 20:00 on Saturdays.

The quietest season of the year. Because sunset falls at 17:15–17:30, the last stop is swapped from Gyeongju National Museum to the Donggung & Wolji night view — you watch it from dusk through to the lights coming on, and this is the only season it is possible. Woljeonggyo also catches the sunset light on winter afternoons.

pdNotes: All three pickup and drop-off points are subway station exits — Busan Station Exit 4 (Line 1), Seomyeon Station Exit 4 (Lines 1 & 2), Haeundae Station Exit 5 (Line 2). At Busan Station we meet at the subway exit in front of the building, NOT inside the KTX railway terminal. Choose the exit closest to your hotel when you book. The tour runs year-round; in cherry blossom season (mid-March to mid-April) Ahopsan Bamboo Forest is replaced by Haeundae Dalmaji Hill, and in winter (Nov–Feb) the last stop changes from Gyeongju National Museum to the Donggung & Wolji night view.
lunchWhyOnRoute: This is where you sit down after Bulguksa's steps and uneven stone, back in central Gyeongju. The afternoon is **covered on foot in two blocks** (Gyochon and the Choi Family House → Woljeonggyo, then Daereungwon → Hwangnidan-gil), so resting properly here is what sets the pace for the rest of the day. The restaurant serves **ssambap**, the local Gyeongju style, and vegetarian or allergy requests are arranged if you flag them the day before. The 55–60 minutes allotted mean nobody has to hurry — restrooms included.

Provide a WhatsApp or KakaoTalk number at booking; the guide will message vehicle details the day before.
walking: Total walking distance across the day is ≈5–5.5 km — more than the previous course, because the two afternoon blocks (Gyochon ↔ Woljeonggyo, Daereungwon ↔ Hwangnidan-gil) are linked on foot.
Bulguksa has stone steps between terraces. Gyochon, Woljeonggyo, Daereungwon and Hwangnidan-gil are all flat, and Daereungwon's grass paths are comfortable for strollers and older guests.
Climbing the tomb mounds is prohibited (fines apply). Comfortable closed-toe shoes essential — Bulguksa stone is uneven.
inclusions: Round-trip mini-van transport from Busan, certified English/Chinese-speaking guide, fuel/tolls/parking.

Not included: lunch (≈₩15,000–₩25,000), Ahopsan Bamboo Forest admission (₩5,000, paid on site), Cheonmachong interior (adult ₩3,000, optional), Donggung & Wolji admission on winter departures (adult ₩3,000), tips.

All other site admissions are free: Bulguksa (free since May 2023), Gyeongju National Museum permanent exhibitions (free since 2008), Gyochon Hanok Village and the Choi Family House, Woljeonggyo Bridge, the Daereungwon park grounds, Hwangnidan-gil.
seasonalAccordion: Cherry blossom season (mid-March to mid-April; exact dates vary year-to-year): Ahopsan Bamboo Forest is replaced by Haeundae Dalmaji Hill, Busan's coastal cherry-tunnel road. The cherry blossoms on Daereungwon's stone-wall lane peak in early April.

Winter (November–February): because sunset falls at 17:15–17:30, the last stop is swapped from Gyeongju National Museum to the Donggung & Wolji night view (admission adult ₩3,000, paid on site). It is the hour that runs from dusk to the lights coming on.
In summer (June–August) sunset is around 19:30, so a night-view stop does not work and the last stop stays fixed as Gyeongju National Museum.

faqReplace.question: Will we see Woljeonggyo Bridge illuminated at night?
faqReplace.answer: On this tour you see Woljeonggyo in daylight, because we arrive around 2 pm together with Gyochon Hanok Village and the Choi Family House — and the timber joinery detail and the reflections on the river are actually clearer by day, with none of the sunset crowd. If you want the illumination, book a winter departure (Nov–Feb): in that season the last stop becomes the Donggung & Wolji night view, so you see Gyeongju's most famous night scene right at the hour the lights come on.

faqReplace.question: Is there English signage in Gyeongju National Museum?
faqReplace.answer: Yes. Major exhibits carry bilingual Korean/English panels, and a recent renovation added digital labels. The permanent exhibitions are free, hours are 10:00–18:00 (last admission 17:30), and regular closures are Jan 1, Seollal and Chuseok only — so it is open as normal on Mondays. This tour arrives around 17:00 and spends 60 minutes on the highlights: the gold crown, the Emille Bell and the Wolji Hall. Winter departures (Nov–Feb) replace the museum with the Donggung & Wolji night view.

faqReplace.question: What's the recommended minimum age?
faqReplace.answer: Best fit is around age 8 and up. The day covers ≈5–5.5 km of walking and runs ≈11.5 hours (08:10 first pickup, ≈19:50 last drop), so a child needs to be comfortable with that rhythm. The two afternoon blocks are actually the kid-friendliest part of the day — Daereungwon is flat, step-free lawn paths with room to move, and Hwangnidan-gil has cafes and Hwangnam bread. The museum's quiet galleries and the early start are the harder parts for young children.

faqReplace.question: How does the day flow?
faqReplace.answer: The morning is two places reached by road; the afternoon is two blocks covered on foot. You leave the three Busan subway stations between 08:10 and 09:10, then Ahopsan Bamboo Forest (60 min) → Bulguksa (75 min) → lunch in central Gyeongju (60 min) closes out the morning. In the afternoon the van stops only twice — from Gyochon Hanok Village and the Choi Family House across the Namcheon to Woljeonggyo (75 min), and from the Daereungwon tombs over one wall into Hwangnidan-gil (75 min). The last slot belongs to the season: March to October it is Gyeongju National Museum (arriving ≈17:00, ahead of its 17:30 last admission), and November to February that same hour is the night-view hour, so it becomes Donggung & Wolji. Drop-off in Busan is Haeundae Station ≈19:15, Seomyeon Station ≈19:35 and Busan Station ≈19:50 — ≈11.5 hours in total.

faqReplace.question: Is this a good choice for first-time visitors to Gyeongju?
faqReplace.answer:
Yes. The day covers Gyeongju's headline sites at an unhurried pace, which suits a first visit well. What makes the difference is that the two afternoon blocks are walked — from the Choi Family House across to Woljeonggyo, and from the Daereungwon mounds over one wall into Hwangnidan-gil — so you come away having seen the texture of the city, not just a checklist of monuments. 

That said, if you want an early evening return, this is not the tour for you: the day runs ≈11.5 hours and Busan drop-offs are 19:15–19:50. In that case a shorter Busan-area tour is the better choice.

faqReplace.question: How much walking is there?
faqReplace.answer: ≈5–5.5 km across the day. It grew from the previous version of this route because both afternoon blocks are now linked on foot — Gyochon to Woljeonggyo along the Namcheon (10–15 min), and Daereungwon out through its west gate into Hwangnidan-gil. Bulguksa is the most active part (uneven stone, gentle uphill); Daereungwon's grass paths are flat and step-free; the museum is flat indoor walking. Comfortable closed-toe shoes essential.

faqReplace.question: Can older adults join comfortably?
faqReplace.answer: Recommended for active seniors comfortable with ≈5–5.5 km of walking and uneven stone at Bulguksa. The afternoon is easier than the distance suggests — Daereungwon is flat, step-free lawn, and Hwangnidan-gil has plenty of cafes to sit down in. Do be aware the day is long: ≈11.5 hours, with drop-off back in Busan around 19:50.

faqReplace.question: Are admissions included?
faqReplace.answer:
Most are free. Free: Bulguksa (since May 2023), the Gyeongju National Museum permanent exhibition (since 2008), Gyochon Hanok Village and the Choi Family House, Woljeonggyo Bridge, the Daereungwon park grounds, and Hwangnidan-gil. 

Paid on site: Ahopsan Bamboo Forest ₩5,000 (required) · the Cheonmachong tomb interior ₩3,000 inside Daereungwon (optional — you can walk the mounds without going in) · on winter departures (Nov–Feb) the last stop changes, so Donggung & Wolji ₩3,000 · lunch ₩15,000–₩25,000. 

Typical total out-of-pocket per person therefore runs about ₩20,000–₩33,000 in summer and about ₩23,000–₩36,000 in winter.

faqReplace.question: What if it rains?
faqReplace.answer:
Light rain: the tour runs as planned. 

Heavy rain: Bulguksa's stone steps get slippery and Ahopsan's earth paths get muddy, so the guide trims outdoor dwell and shifts the balance indoors. From March to October that means more time at Gyeongju National Museum — still the last stop, indoors and climate-controlled — and at Daereungwon less time among the mounds in exchange for more time in Hwangnidan-gil's indoor cafes and shops. In winter (Nov–Feb) the last stop is the open-air Donggung & Wolji pond, so in rain it can be swapped back to the museum, provided arrival still clears the 17:30 last admission. 

Typhoon-grade weather: rescheduling or a full refund.

faqAdd.question: What do we do on Hwangnidan-gil?
faqAdd.answer: It is a street of cafes, studios and gift shops converted out of hanok houses, directly across Daereungwon's west wall. The name means 'Hwangnam-dong's Gyeongnidan-gil', and since around 2017 it has been the youngest street in Gyeongju. You get roughly 20–30 minutes of free time — enough for a coffee, a box of Hwangnam bread (the red-bean pastry that started in this neighbourhood in 1939), and a restroom stop. Anything you buy is at your own expense.

faqAdd.question: Do I miss Gyeongju National Museum if I go in winter?
faqAdd.answer: Yes — on Nov–Feb departures the last stop is replaced by the Donggung & Wolji night view. In winter the sun is already low by around 5 pm, which shortens a museum visit, while that same hour is exactly when Gyeongju's best night view begins. The two sites are 5 minutes apart by car, and since the 33,000-plus artifacts in the museum's Wolji Hall came out of the bed of that very pond, the story still connects. If the museum is essential for you, choose a departure between March and October.

faqAdd.question: Is the pickup point a train station or a subway station?
faqAdd.answer: All three are subway station exits — Busan Station Exit 4 (Subway Line 1), Seomyeon Station Exit 4 (Lines 1 & 2), Haeundae Station Exit 5 (Line 2). At Busan Station in particular we meet at Exit 4 of the subway station in front of the building, not inside the KTX railway terminal. If you wait in the train station concourse or on the plaza you will not see the vehicle, so please navigate by the subway exit number. Drop-off is at the same three points.

bulguksaWhyOnRoute: Bulguksa is **the essential UNESCO anchor of any Gyeongju day tour** and the most widely recognized Buddhist heritage site in Korea. The 11:30 arrival comes after the morning's Korean school groups have cleared — they generally fill the courtyards between roughly 09:30 and 11:00 — so the temple grounds are noticeably quieter by the time you walk in. The 75 minutes allotted are enough to follow the full pilgrimage route without hurrying the **Dabotap and Seokgatap** pair. This is also **the last stop of the morning reached by van**: after lunch the van stops only twice, and the afternoon is spent on foot. And because Bulguksa's stone steps and uneven ground are the most active stretch of the whole day, lunch follows immediately — so guests actually sit down.
lunchDescription:
Lunch comes as the van moves from Bulguksa into central Gyeongju, at a local restaurant picked by the guide. The signature dish is **Gyeongju-style ssambap** (rice with seasonal banchan and lettuce wraps — a local meal style that became widely known in the 1970s, reflecting the region's agricultural abundance). 

**Vegetarian and allergy requests are arranged if you flag them the day before.** The meal is not included in the tour price and runs **about ₩15,000–₩25,000 per person**. The 60 minutes allotted let you eat and use the restrooms without watching the clock — **because the afternoon is spent walking two blocks**, resting properly here is what sets the pace for the rest of the day.
lunchHighlights: Guide-picked local restaurant in central Gyeongju
**Gyeongju-style ssambap** — rice with seasonal banchan and lettuce wraps
**Vegetarian and allergy requests** arranged if flagged the day before
**60 minutes allotted** — the proper rest before the afternoon's two walked blocks
Cost about **₩15,000–₩25,000** per person, NOT included in the tour price
